Title: Tactics Tuesdays: Prefacing | Girls Chase
chunks: Prefacing lets you approach women or issues in ways that they'd push back on otherwise… yet, with you, thanks to you prefacing, they accept (& even enjoy!). Tiny little tactic here that lets you get away with lots. Generally there are some subjects in conversation you cannot touch. Certain sensitivities, criticisms, or, alternately, certain proposals. Things that if you accuse someone of them or suggest them raise so many hackles it can blow the whole conversation up. Sometimes, too, you'll meet hot-tempered people quick to jump to conclusions every time you manage to utter more than a few syllables. These individuals can be particularly hard to talk to, as they personalize nearly everything you say. Finally, there are things you might say – including many of the openers you deliver to women during cold approach – that might be hard to swallow on their own. They seem incongruent or hard to believe. A woman might think you're just yanking her chain. The one tactic you can use to route around each and every one of these problems is prefacing; where you use a short prefacing statement to pace your listener's understanding before diving into the juicy stuff. Prefacing Examples Let me start with an example just so make the tactic clear. Let's say you're talking to a girl and she seems a bit anal-retentive and hasn't bitten so far on any of the sexual topics you've floated. You want to try a little gambit about being ‘sexually stiff' to see if that loosens her up. However, you suspect if you just accuse her of it or talk about it on its own, without prefacing, she'll reject it. For instance: YOU: You know, I've noticed certain people tend to be pretty ‘sexually stiff'.

They have a lot of rules they follow and are generally a lot more suspicious of sexual things. It's my belief these people cut themselves off from a lot of themselves. HER: I don't know what you're talking about. I don't think that's true at all. She will reject it because she feels like you're accusing her without accusing her. Your statement doesn't name her, so she'd look defensive if she just blurted out “Not me!”; instead she simply rejects the premise whole cloth; a kind of ‘nuke it from orbit' move. What if instead you tell her directly you're talking about her, still without prefacing? YOU: You know, it seems like you might be one of the people I judge to be pretty ‘sexually stiff'. Such people have a lot of rules they follow and are generally a lot more suspicious of sexual things. It's my belief these people cut themselves off from a lot of themselves. HER: You're wrong. You don't know anything about me. A direct accusation runs a high risk of turning the girl defensive and causing her to reject your suggestion. Once again, the approach does not work. What can we do if we want to use this gambit? We can preface it… by telling the girl it is not about her. YOU: I'm not saying this is you, but I've noticed certain people tend to be pretty ‘sexually stiff'. They have a lot of rules they follow and are generally a lot more suspicious of sexual things. It's my belief these people cut themselves off from a lot of themselves. HER: I think that's true. Some people are just not as comfortable with sexual things. And now you're in and can talk about being easier-going sexually.

Because you prefaced it by telling her you are “not saying this is” her, you avoid the kneejerk “I'm being accused!” reaction… and now she reacts toward it differently. Also, because you've extended her the benefit of the doubt (by “not assuming” anything about her), she is socially obligated to do the same to you, extending you the benefit of the doubt as your observation extended her (that your statement is about “certain people” more generally) and not dismissing it out-of-hand. The reaction most of the time is either going to be: She agrees that it is true and certain people are sexually unconfident, OR She starts to qualify herself: “Yes, and just to be clear I am really not that way” or “I actually am that way a little bit” Each of those responses works to your benefit: her agreeing with the statement opens it up for conversation; her qualifying herself puts you firmly in the lead. But why would adding just a few little words of prefacing completely change the way a statement is received? The Power of Similarity & Attainability The more similar she feels to you, and the more attainable, the more being with you is like being with a nice, warm, fluffy pillow she can snuggle right up to — instead of a cold, unfeeling man she needs to stay away from. We use prefacing before anything we say that might make a girl feel we are too dissimilar to her and thus unattainable for her. If you're talking to a girl and out of the blue accuse her of sexual woodenness, she will very likely be offended, feel like you do not ‘get' her, feel like your and her values are too dissimilar, and begin to auto-reject you.

If you approach a woman cold and jump right into a too-polished opener, she will think you must do this all the time, feel like you and her are completely different (SHE would certainly never go around talking to lots of strangers all the time! It's just weird!), feel like your and her values are too dissimilar, and begin to auto-reject you. Readers of my book How to Make Girls Chase are intimately familiar with how big a role attainability plays in the success or failure of your seductions. If a woman starts to feel that you are not attainable to her – i.e., that you do not really respect her, that the interaction is not actually ‘real' in some way, or that a girl like her cannot actually get a guy like you – she will auto-reject you to protect her ego. One Date owners know how vital it is to maintain a feeling of shared underlying attitudes with women you're talking to. So long as she feels the two of you share similar attitudes toward life, she will trust you, and the interaction flows smoothly along. But if she begins to suspect that your and her attitudes are too dissimilar, trust erodes, you become unattainable, and the interaction falls apart. Prefaces allow you to avoid ‘accidental similarity/attainability damage' with statements and approaches that are otherwise ‘too out there' from a girl's usual point of view. That is how you're able to get away with things you otherwise could not by prefacing. As an example: say you approach a girl on the street and tell her, “Excuse, but you're REALLY pretty and I had to meet you. I'm Liam.” Now, she may be flattered, and she may stop and talk.

Nevertheless, it's so out-of-the-blue and un-prefaced that she is going to wonder who does that? Who just walks up to a random stranger to compliment her like that? Well, most of the guys who have done it to her in the past were thirsty guys, desperate guys, or horny guys, so she'll be tempted to throw you into their lot. Unless she's a little thirsty and horny herself, that is going to make her feel like you and her are on different wavelengths. -attainability -similarity and you're already starting off on the wrong foot. But if instead you preface your opener, you can have a completely different effect: YOU: Excuse me… [authoritative voice tone; 2-3 second pause to let her to wonder what you have to say; curious smile as if there is something very interesting about her] but I saw you sitting here, and I simply HAD to come tell you, that… [1-2 second pause + genuine interest nose crinkle] you have the sunniest disposition I have seen all day. Like I can just feel the sunbeams pouring off of you. I'm Chase. Anything where you suspect her default reaction will be to push back and tell you “No way!” or “No thanks.” Some examples of non-opener prefaces: “I'm not saying this is you, but” “Now don't take this the wrong way, however” “I'm going to talk about XYZ but that's not an accusation” “I'm not saying we need to do this, but WHAT IF…” For instance: You're talking to a girl at a party who is moody and difficult. You tell her, “I'm not saying this is you, but have you noticed how some people go out to have fun but then they don't let themselves have fun? Why do you think that is?” She can: Comment on how OTHER people do that… and now she will feel social pressure to also display (through lightening up her behavior) how she herself is NOT that way.

Acknowledge that she IS doing it, tell you WHY, then still feel social pressure (now that she's admitted to it) to lighten up a bit and not be so pouty. (bonus: there's an implicit conformity frame embedded there, as you suggest that the “thing everybody does” at parties is have fun, but she by not doing it is the odd one out) Or let's say you're sitting in a park talking with a girl. The conversation is pleasant but platonic. This girl has an amazing posterior though and you keep glancing at it / thinking about it. You feel like it'd be better to just say something rather than say nothing and let this keep on being platonic. But you don't want to sound like a complete horndog. So, you preface: “Now, don't take this the wrong way, however you have just an amazing ass. Just throwing that out there!” If she likes you, she is going to laugh and engage with this. She may well start to be a lot more flirtatious with you, as she may not have realized before that it was supposed to be a flirtation, that she was ‘allowed' to flirt, or that you even liked her that way (maybe you seemed a bit too high value and did not seem attainable to her. Now imagine this scenario: you're hours into a seduction with a girl, and it's going well but beginning to feel stale. You want to propose a move but she's been a little resistant compliance-wise and you're not certain she'll go for it.

Had you just told her, “Let's go to the pond and go skinny dipping,” it would not have matched the dynamic, would feel like you are not attuned to her ‘resistant' wavelength at all, and would hurt both similarity and attainability. But because you preface it as a ‘crazy idea' that you are simply floating rather than demanding, she can either laugh it off as a joke or accept it as a thing to do. If she laughs it off as a joke (“You're crazy!”) it nevertheless implants a sexual frame in her head and at the same time suggests that you want to get things moving, so she'd better quit dragging her feet. If she accepts it (“You know what… why not. Okay!”) then you break out of the rut you were in and stand an excellent chance of nailing this chick naked in the lake. Let's say you brought it up a few times already but she hasn't fixed it and gets defensive when you bring it up. You need to figure out what she's feeling accused of being, then preface that you are NOT accusing her of that, then tell her WHAT you want her to do. Title: Operant Conditioning: Response Size & Big Picture Focus | Girls Chase
chunks: Operant conditioning (or behavior shaping) lets you modify how people act through rewards and punishments. But in ‘mixed case' scenarios things get tricky… I first wrote about operant conditioning a dozen years ago in my article on using for behavior shaping inside romantic relationships. If you haven't read that one, or it's been a while, read it first, because this article builds upon it. The quick summary is that through rewards and punishment, you can direct another person's behavior. Reward her, and you'll get more of that behavior. Punish her, and you'll get less of it. Today's article focuses on some nuance in operant conditioning. Namely: how the size of your response affects reinforcement/discouragement… plus the importance of focusing on the big picture too rather than exclusively the small one. Big vs. Little Picture Behavior Shaping Oftentimes in behavior shaping, you will encounter complex situations. For instance, a woman may make a mistake inside the broader context of doing something aimed at helping you. Here's an example: let's say you want to take a day trip together. You task her with planning it out. She eagerly handles the planning, happy to invest in your relationship this way. The big day comes, and the two of you drive far out of town. After a fun day of touring about, you arrive at the hotel she planned out… only to discover the place no longer exists. It was demolished two years ago. It is now nighttime, you're in the middle of nowhere, tired from a day of trekking, and there are no other hotels nearby. Making things worse, you've heard of highwaymen in the area setting up traps for lonely travelers driving the dark roads at night.

People have been rolling along, only to come upon a truck parked in the middle of the road, blocking it. Sometimes someone may be laying on the road, seemingly injured. Meanwhile, other robbers lie in wait along the shoulder of the road, hiding themselves until the victims exit their vehicle to investigate. You're thinking about all this, tired, stressed, and your woman is starting to panic to boot. What is the right response from an operant conditioning perspective? She needs punishment to avoid future situations like this (i.e., not ensuring a crucial destination still, in fact, exists). However, that is not the only consideration here, because there is both a BIG picture and a SMALL one. The small picture is “your woman brought you to a hotel in the middle of nowhere that no longer exists.” The big picture is “your woman did a lot of research to put this entire day trip together, investing in you and the relationship.” If you punish severely (such as getting extremely annoyed at her), you punish BOTH the mistake of bringing you to the missing hotel AND the investment of planning out the whole day trip. You will teach her to be more careful, yes. However, you will also condition her to not be so eager to invest in you or the relationship. The latter is a big problem you probably did not intend – but will give yourself to deal with regardless! Response Size Affects Attribution I have not seen tests on this, but my experience has led me to conclude that the bigger the response, the bigger the attribution.

That is to say, if you give the day trip-planning girl a small, measured punishment, she will tie that to the immediate thing (missing hotel), and likely learn to plan trips more carefully in the future. However, if you give her a LARGE, SEVERE punishment, she will tie that to the big picture item (her planning out the entire day trip), and learn to turn down opportunities to invest in the relationship like this instead of eagerly take them on. In other words: You sigh deeply and say, “This is trouble. We're in the middle of nowhere, in a region that has bandits, we're tired, it's dark, and this hotel does not exist. The rest of the trip was excellent, but this is not good.” She gets specific, measured punishment that makes her more likely to be careful in her research in the future. OR You freak out, yelling, screaming, and ranting, banging your hands on the steering wheel, cursing, totally out of control. Maybe you loudly ask, “Why did I ever leave this to you?” making her feel as if the entire trip has been a complete disaster. She gets large, severe punishment that she is going to tie to the entire trip, making her more likely to avoid planning day trips in the future, wanting to go on day trips, or really invest in the relationship with you more generally. If the response is large, the attribution moves to the BIG PICTURE. That's no problem when both big picture and little picture are both bad. For instance, if she went out partying without you, then got drunk and you had to call her a taxi. When she got to your place you were furious.

The message she gets is not “getting drunk when I go out is painful” (little picture) but rather “going out to party without my man is painful” (big picture). That serves your aims too – unless you want your girl going out to party without you (maybe some dudes do?). However, when the situation is mixed – such as when the big picture is good (she was doing something to be helpful) but the little picture is bad (she messed up) – you must be very careful what response size you use IF you do not want to discourage the big picture good behavior. Why People Tune Out of Relationships A precipitating factor in why people leave. Disproportionate response sizes that accidentally punish good big picture behavior are an important reason people ‘tune out' of long-term relationships, in my experience. The stereotype of the henpecked husband who spends more and more time at work, avoiding being around his family, or the deadbeat dad who one day goes out for milk and never comes back, are examples of this. People don't one day tune out or one day leave because “they were just bored” (well, not normally, anyway). They do it because they reached a breaking point where they felt their efforts were too thankless, or even felt actively resented. What often happens in these relationships is the man tries to do what he thinks is good (investing in the relationship – what the woman wants!), only to do something that is not done the way the woman wants, or he overlooks something the woman thinks is important, or otherwise fails to meet her expectations, and she gives him lots of drama.

Because the response size is disproportionate to the offense, and does not account for the mixed scenario of “good big picture, bad little picture”, the man learns the ultimate lesson that “investing in relationship = bad” and reduces his investment levels (which, ultimately, frustrates the woman even more, leading to more drama, more punishment, and more tuning out on the man's part). But men often do this too; particularly hot-tempered men. If you are a hot-tempered man you must be very careful about this. When you punish a woman too severely for messing up on a detail when she was trying to serve you/the relationship, the ultimate effect is that you train her not to serve you or the relationship. In other words, you are causing her to tune out of the relationship. That is probably NOT what you want. But no matter WHAT you WANT, it WILL be the effect, if the response size is disproportionate, and the ‘training scenario' is mixed! Dealing with Mixed Scenario Punishment/Reward These considerations only matter for genuine ‘mixed scenarios'. That is: Big picture good, little picture bad (planned whole day trip, but messed up hotel) Big picture bad, little picture good (went out to drink with the girls, but home early) Especially if you are hot-tempered or present time-oriented, you are going to tend to prioritize the most immediate (little picture) item and ignore the overarching (big picture) context. Examples: You blow up at her for messing up the hotel. The lesson she learns? “Don't agree to plan day trips or invest so much in the relationship. It hurts! Not worth it!” You gush over her for how responsible she is coming home early from a night out drinking with the girls. The lesson she learns?

“It's totally cool to go out drinking without him. I even get bonus points with him if I manage to get home early!” In the first example, you inadvertently discourage her from investing more in the relationship. In the second example, you inadvertently encourage her going out to drink without you. Both of these are mistakes, assuming you want girls to invest in you and don't want them going out partying and drinking. READ MORE: Why I Quit Dating Girls Who Club, Party, or Drink How should you respond to these scenarios? With a deliberately muted, controlled response. You HAVE to! You MUST be aware of the double condition – one element good, the other element bad. You do not want to discourage good behavior, but you also don't want to encourage bad. So: When she screws up the hotel, you control yourself, reminding yourself she planned the whole trip, and just express moderate, measured disappointment. “Welp, this is bad.” If she's clearly already stressed, you keep punishment very light (she is already self-punishing); if she's blissfully ignorant as to how bad the situation is, you apply a little more pressure, while still keeping it measured – she needs to know she screwed up, but that is was just on this one thing, not everything. When she comes home early after going out drinking, again, you control yourself, not gushing in relief but giving her a measured, “I'm glad you didn't stay out too late,” that approves of her return but still shows disapproval overall that she went out in the first place. This way she gets the message that “Coming home early was good, but it'd be better had I not gone out at all.”

The muted, measured response is KEY for any mixed behavior shaping situation you find yourself in. It is absolutely essential to avoid sending the wrong message and ‘mistraining' her. Mixed Scenarios Are Common. Always Look at the Big Picture! How guilty is she, and what is the context? Let that be the guide to your response size. You need to get yourself into the habit of examining behaviors in light of the context they occur within. Most small behaviors occur in the context of a larger overarching pattern. People make mistakes when they are trying to do good things. They also do good things in the midst of overall misbehaving. If you only address the immediate item, and if you do so in a strong or severe way, you risk shaping behavior in the wrong direction: punish good behavior, or reward bad behavior. Always examine the meta-context of a behavior: Was the good behavior done in a bad larger context? Do not give gushing praise. Was the bad behavior done in a good larger context? Do not mete out harsh punishment. This is how you avoid worsening bad behaviors accidentally, or discouraging good behaviors accidentally. Many a relationship has been sabotaged by discouraging good behaviors or permitting bad ones. Don't make that mistake – always keep the context top of mind! Title: Tactics Tuesdays: Conformity Framing | Girls Chase
chunks: If you want to get a girl to do what you want, it's a lot easier if she thinks what you want is ‘what everyone is doing' or ‘what the cool kids do'. That's conformity framing. Women are herd creatures. Women, far more than men, feel driven to conform. This can work against your interests when the direction of their conformity goes against your desires. For instance: She's consuming a lot of messages about how important it is to “not sleep with a man too quickly.” So she puts up many more walls to sleeping with you. She's part of a friend group that talks down on men working the trades. However, you work a trade. When she finds this out, she loses attraction to you. All her social circle is filled with party people who drink and do drugs and think anyone who doesn't is a stick in the mud. You're a teetotaler. So, she decides you're boring. Other women with other perspectives might find you sexy and exciting (and be highly willing to comply with you!). But because these girls are operating within paradigms where they believe the ‘consensus' is to reject your advances or look down on you/your traits/lifestyle, you run into walls with them. What can you do about this? Well, one tool in our seducer's toolbox is this: you can frame what YOU want or are as the consensus, and shift her paradigm to one that aligns with you. Conformity Seriously Impacts a LOT with Girls I've talked at times about my experiences with picking up blonde bombshells. These are girls who bleach their hair blonde (despite not being natural blondes) and dress and act in the most stereotypically ‘cool' ways they can. Such gals are conformists through and through.

When I first started picking up girls, blonde bombshells were the coldest of any girls I approached. They'd continually snub me and act disinterested in me. Eventually I came to dislike and avoid them. No other type of girl treated me like that – just these stuck-up bombshells! I didn't know what the cause was, until one day I began to wonder if it might be due to these girls' conformist natures – plus me not matching the ‘stereotypical cool/sexy guy' look or vibe. My look and vibe were good… but not ‘trendy dude sexy' good. So, I changed my look, adopting trendy facial hair, a trendy hairstyle, and cool, trendy clothes, and ALMOST INSTANTLY blonde bombshells warmed right up to me. Suddenly I was the guy these girls wanted to meet; they found me fascinating, loved flirting and talking with me, and started coming home with me. “That's it?” I wondered. “It is really just down to IMAGE?” I shouldn't have been surprised. My adventures with social experimentation started in sixth grade. One day when I was 12 years old, I switched to wearing a popular sports team's coat, removed my glasses, and behaved more extroverted. The result: my classmates en masse saw me in a completely different light. They began treating me totally different too (way better, in fact. I went from “nerd” to “interesting and cool” in a single day). The reason why is because when you CONFORM with what people think is ‘cool', ‘sexy', ‘popular', or ‘expected', people naturally view you as being those things and treat you as such.

Girls will quickly sleep with guys who match the image that is already in their head of ‘sexy bad boy girls sleep with fast', while avoiding fast sex with guys who match the image in their head of ‘reliable safe guy girls take it slow with'. It almost does not matter what else you say or do; if you match the image, you get treated like the image! Conformity with certain stereotypes and conceptions has a LARGE effect on how your seductions play out. But what do you do if you are already dressed how you're dressed, have behaved how you've behaved, and now you're running up against a wall where girls give you resistance to conform to some set of beliefs they ‘believe' they ‘should'? Conformity Framing: “All the Cool Kids Are Doing It” There are many forces in society that want her to behave in certain ways. No doubt you've heard those lines, used to convince other people to do something, of: “Come on… everyone is doing it.” Or “All the cool kids are doing it.” These lines often feel like bald, blatant manipulation… and YET, despite their obviousness, they often work. In high school and college, I had other kids use these lines on me, and sometimes I'd comply! Other times I'd still resist, but I'd feel enormous pressure as I resisted it, because I felt like I was making myself look lame or uncool. I'm a lot more resistant to social pressure and external influence than most people are. But these obvious lines have still worked on me! These lines are conformity framing. They attempt to frame something as ‘cool', ‘accepted', or ‘ubiquitous'.

They seek to get someone to change his or her behavior by framing that person's behavior as ‘uncool', ‘outsider', or ‘weird' to make that person want to switch to the comparatively more accepted, cool, normal behavior. Other typical conformity framing lines you may have heard: “It's [current year]. This is normal now.” “You're [age]. You should be comfortable with this by now.” “You're never going to [something good] with that attitude!” “Really? You're not comfortable with [desired thing]?” “Is this new for you? Have you not done this before?” All these conformity frames work by placing social pressure on the individual to ‘get with it' or otherwise show that he or she is not uncool, left behind, and outsider, but is just as cool and hip as other people are. While these lines can work, they're a bit ‘dark side' for my taste. Also a bit too naked in their intent, and more prone to making people resent you and see you as a manipulator after the fact. Instead, what I prefer is a more holistic approach to conformity framing, where you take a woman on a small journey that helps her understand how something actually is the norm, and that it is okay to engage in it. Fleshed Out Conformity Frames Here's a more ‘fleshed out' conformity frame. Let's say you're with a girl who's resistant to going to bed with you. You talk to her and it comes up that “everyone says you shouldn't hop into bed with a man too quick. It makes him not respect you as much and leads to regret.” The best way (in my opinion) to turn the conformity frame in your advantage is this process: Find out where she's getting this conformity frame from.

Dismiss the frame as being pushed by a vocal minority. Share the REAL conformity frame (“everyone is doing it”). Discuss some of the benefits of what the thing is. Then reiterate that these benefits are why everyone is doing it. If necessary, show her (better than telling her) examples of people doing it. With the girl who says “everyone says you shouldn't hop into bed with a man too quick”, you might have this conversation: YOU: [escalating on her] HER: [resisting you] YOU: What's holding you back? HER: It's just that everyone says you shouldn't hop into bed with a man too quick. It makes him not respect you as much and leads to regret. YOU: Who says that? [STEP 1: find out where her conformity frame comes from] HER: Like influencers and stuff. Some of my friends say it too. YOU: These influencers are all like parrots. One of them says something then they all repeat it because that's what gets the most clicks. It's not real consensus; it's what Edward Bernays called ‘manufactured consensus'. Then regular people see it and parrot it, like those friends of yours. [STEP 2: dismiss her conformity frame as pushed by a vocal minority] Most people get together when they want to get together. They don't follow some rules from a handful of vocal influencers on social media. [STEP 3: share the REAL conformity frame] They follow their hearts, do what feels right, and don't block themselves off from the connections, and pleasure, and release they desire with someone they desire it with. [STEP 4: discuss benefits of the real popular thing] That's why most people do not do what these anal-retentive vocal minority people working as ‘influencers' say, where they all just parrot each other.

[STEP 5: reiterate these benefits are why ‘everyone is doing it'] HER: Maybe, but I'm just not sure. YOU: Look, didn't we JUST see your friend Lucy go home with a guy tonight? What do you think they went home to do, play checkers? [STEP 6: show her examples of other people doing it] HER: [laugh] YOU: This is natural. This is what people do. People get attracted to each other, and they get together. They do not wait for some unspecified timer to go off that says, “Okay, enough time has passed! Now it is allowed!” There are not following the commands of some tiny minority of rigid influencers say. HER: I guess you're right. YOU: You know I'm right [wink]. [make out; escalation continues] When you build a properly fleshed out conformity frame like this, that busts up a girl's preexisting conformity frame and installs a new one in her, you leave much less room for doubt that you are ‘manipulating' her and make it much clearer that, in fact, the frame you're pushing really IS what ‘everyone is doing' – it is not just a thing that you're saying to her. Conformity Framing Is a Tool; It Is Not the Whole Seduction Conformity framing relieves her of the fear that doing what you want is “not conforming.” But you still must seduce her in other ways, too. One thing I want to point out here is that conformity framing is a tactic you can use; it is not the entire seduction in and of itself. For instance, with the girl giving resistance to quick escalation, you have successfully reframed quick sex as the REAL thing that ‘everyone is doing', which removes that objection from her to hooking up (“Oh, okay. This is accepted, actually.

This is the normal thing that people do”). However, if she still has other objections, you will need to handle those as well. If she doesn't feel similar enough to you, aroused enough by you, you have not escalated compliance enough, etc., or has other points of resistance, you will need to handle those. Conformity framing is a very useful tactic; just keep in mind that it is one tactic to be used in conjunction with the rest of your usual seduction repertoire. Treat it that way (rather than as a magic pill to seduce girls all by itself) and you will find it helps you clear away obstacles that other tactics and approaches can have difficulty overcoming. Chase Amante

Title: What to Do After Unprotected Sex | Girls Chase
chunks: Things got a little too frisky and in a moment of passion you left protection aside. What steps should you take after the act to ensure you stay clean? Hey guys. Welcome back. Note: This post addresses the aftermath of unprotected sex, which is a scary experience for some individuals. If you are in this situation, please read this post; it is for you. The sooner you read it, the better off you will be. In my two most recent posts, I covered the important and often uncomfortable subject of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), discussing what they are and how to prevent them. These posts contain valuable information beyond what is typically found on standard sex education websites. I cover methods such as PrEP, a medication that helps prevent HIV, as well as one that helps reduce contracting gonorrhea. Additionally, I highlight some lesser-known facts about various STIs. I encourage you to check out these posts for more insights. In my opinion, a playboy must educate himself about STIs. It is important to understand them and learn how to prevent their transmission; condoms are just one of many tools at your disposal. Prevention methods not only safeguard your own health but also protect others. As a playboy, you increase your risk of exposure, putting others at risk as well. It is essential to master this knowledge for everyone's safety. Please remember that although I have written these posts, I am not a health care professional—just someone who has done considerable research. The purpose of these posts is to provide an overview of available information and help you understand your options. With this knowledge, you can consult your doctor or health care professional to discuss your best choices. Their expertise takes precedence over mine.

In this post, I will discuss the aftermath of unprotected sex. Say an accident happened; perhaps the condom broke, or you were swept up in the moment and forgot to protect yourself. Now, it's the next day, and paranoia has set in. Regardless of how you're feeling—anxious or indifferent—this guide will help you understand what steps to take next. Forgetting the Condom: Am I Screwed? It felt so good, but now you're not sure it was the best decision… It's hard to predict whether unprotected sex will cause problems, as it depends on various factors. Diseases such as chlamydia and gonorrhea are common. If you engage in regular unprotected sex, your risk of contracting these infections is high. However, these diseases are curable and typically do not lead to complications if treated. Therefore, it's important to test yourself. What about herpes and HPV? They are more of a nuisance than a serious threat. Protecting yourself against both can be challenging, aside from getting the HPV vaccine; see my post on STI prevention. There is not much you can do to shield yourself fully. While condoms can provide some level of protection, if a girl you have sex with has blisters that come in contact with an unprotected part of your penis, you still face a risk, even when using condoms. I usually do not think about herpes as it is somewhat beyond my control. However, I always make sure to avoid sex if I notice any blisters or sores. What about nasty infections, like hepatitis C and syphilis? Both are serious diseases and can lead to life-threatening complications if not treated effectively. Fortunately, hepatitis C is now curable.

The likelihood of contracting hepatitis C through sex (including anal sex) is relatively low, which is why STI clinics do not routinely test for it. However, there is a risk for transmission if both partners experience bleeding during very rough sex if one partner is hepatitis C-positive. The transmission of hepatitis C through other body fluids is debatable. While I wouldn't be overly concerned, it's still advisable to get tested. Syphilis is a severe infection that can lead to organ failure if left untreated. It is more contagious than hepatitis C. The good news is that syphilis is curable, so get tested and treated. You should take all these infections seriously. Get tested and cured. Most infections cannot be tested immediately due to an incubation period; test results usually won't be positive right away. I will discuss this in detail shortly. There's no need to worry, as serious damage does not occur instantly. It can take months or even years for complications to develop. For example, phase 2 syphilis causes severe damage about one year after exposure. However, the sooner it is treated, the better. Waiting an extra week before getting tested is okay, as this leads to more reliable results. The HIV Scare “How to know if you have HIV” HIV is the infection that worries most individuals. It usually requires treatment for the rest of your life. However, since many get treated, the spread in heterosexual circles in developed countries is limited. HIV can lead to feelings of panic. You may find yourself googling to determine if you are okay or checking the odds of how transmittable and contagious it is. This can be overwhelming. The reality is that most statistics are averages and may not reflect your situation.

The likelihood of contracting HIV depends on several factors: where penetration occurs, whether you are circumcised, if your partner is on medication (which can significantly lower the risk, often close to zero), if her viral load is high (it can be particularly high if she just contracted the virus), and whether either of you has another STI, such as chlamydia. STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia significantly increase your chance of contracting HIV if you have sexual contact with someone who is HIV-positive. These infections can facilitate the transmission of HIV. To reduce risk, ensure that you do not have bacterial STIs such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, or syphilis. Make it a priority to get tested regularly and get treatment when necessary. Here's a fact sheet about transmission rates. As you can see, unless you are being reckless, your odds as a heterosexual man are low. Receptive partners, which include women and many gay men, are more at risk. Remember that the risk is still there, and all it takes is a girl on her period who recently contracted HIV. She may have a high viral load and be very contagious. Your chance of catching infections is much higher. Your odds of being exposed to HIV-positive women increase if you live in an area with a high prevalence of HIV. If you are taking PrEP (a preventive treatment against HIV) as prescribed by your health care provider, the odds are nearly zero. While there have been rare instances of PrEP failures, these are usually due to patients not following the treatment properly. See this article. You can calculate and speculate as much as you like, but it will only cause undue stress. If you catch a cold, you may tell yourself you have it.

You may google “signs of HIV” and “symptoms,” but, likely, you don't have HIV. Symptoms are not a reliable indicator of HIV. GET TESTED. It's as simple as that. I will cover STI testing in my next post, but briefly, it's best to get tested after six weeks. Ask for a fourth-generation test. This tests reliably for both antibodies and antigens (p24). If you are very worried, you can call an HIV hotline and speak with an expert. They can provide information and help assess your situation, which may help calm your nerves. Alternatively, visit a clinic and get a preliminary test after two to three weeks; this can give you a decent indicator of whether you may have HIV. However, you should repeat the test after four weeks for more accurate results. A test conducted six weeks after your potential exposure will give a reliable result with close to 100% accuracy. PEP: Day-After Pills for HIV If you did not plan ahead, there are still ways to cut your risk. Many people are not aware that there is a day-after pill for HIV. In most developed countries, you can access post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which is an anti-retroviral treatment that significantly reduces your chances of contracting HIV if exposed to the virus. While some studies debate its effectiveness, many agree that PEP can reduce the risk of infection by over 80% when used as prescribed. See this article. To maximize its effectiveness. You must take the treatment within 72 hours of exposure, ideally within 24 hours. The prescribing authority varies by location. In some countries, general practitioners prescribe it; this may not be the case in others. Also, your local hospital emergency room may provide PEP. Before you rejoice, there is a catch to PEP.

It is a 28-day treatment of powerful anti-retroviral medication. While it is certainly better than contracting HIV, the treatment can be challenging. It can be expensive, and your insurance may not cover the costs. Typically, a doctor will evaluate your situation to determine if PEP is appropriate. They often prescribe doses for the first few days to get you started. They will schedule a follow-up appointment with an infectious disease specialist to reassess your situation and decide whether you should continue the treatment. They will also monitor your health for the next two to three months. You cannot rely on PEP as a preventive measure. Instead, consider PrEP, which has significantly fewer side effects. PrEP can be taken before and after sex and requires only four pills over three days. For more, refer to my previous article. Here is a valuable resource about PrEP. If you have sex with a riskier group, consider this option. This includes having sex with a woman who is a sex worker or drug user, including snorters. It can be difficult to assess whether a woman is in a risk group or not and whether you are at risk. In those cases, your best bet is to call an HIV hotline, talk to your doctor, or your hospital emergency room. Avoid the 911 emergency number, as it is not a matter of life and death. Questionable Advice Does cleaning up after sex help? Well, it can't hurt. Below are some disputable tips and tricks that may be helpful, but remember that none are scientifically proven. I see no harm in trying them as long as you also get tested and do not substitute them for legitimate protection methods, such as condoms, PrEP, and vaccines. One is to urinate after sex.

This is a good idea, as it may flush out potential bacteria that could cause urinary tract infections. Whether this can help flush out chlamydia and other bacterial STIs is questionable. To my knowledge, there is no scientific evidence to prove it. The same goes for post-sex showers and general clean-up. In theory, this should help. However, it is not scientifically proven to help mitigate STIs. I mention both because men often discuss this advice, and I see it pop up in discussions about STIs on forums. And this does make sense. I doubt there is any harm in peeing and cleaning up after sex for general hygiene. I prefer to wash after sex. It's a personal preference. Parting Words If you had unplanned unprotected sex, be sure to get tested after to make sure you picked nothing up. If you have unprotected sex, it is crucial to assess whether you are exposed to something serious like HIV and act quickly. Contact a medical professional within 72 hours to determine if you should take PEP to decrease your chance of contracting a virus. Other STIs, aside from hepatitis B, are curable. However, hepatitis B has a vaccine available. With hepatitis B out of the way, you can chill out and remain calm. The other STIs are a nonissue as long as you get tested. The exception is herpes. However, herpes is very common, usually not dangerous, and is technically not considered an STI. It is more of a nuisance. If you want to know more about herpes, I have dedicated two posts where I discuss it in depth, including how to live with it and how to date while having it to avoid spreading it to others.

If you fear herpes or struggle with it, please read these posts; they will help: Dating with Herpes, Pt. 1: Dating Strategies Dating with Herpes, Pt. 2: Relationships The next step is to get tested. You can read about how to do that in my article on testing for STIs (link below). Stay safe. Best, Alek READ NEXT: “Getting Tested for STIs: The Active Dater's Guide”

Title: 11 Signs You're an AFC (Average Frustrated Chump) | Girls Chase
chunks: Average Frustrated Chump: an ordinary guy, thwarted with women, falling for silly woman tricks. Here's how to tell if you're AFC – and what to do if so. As I've been on social media (here's our X account), I have come face to face with just how many frustrated, average men there are out there struggling with a lack of dating success. That's nothing new, of course. It's always been this way. But Girls Chase has long served as kind of a bastion due to our large audience of savvy dudes vs. comparatively few very frustrated guys. After wading back onto social media though I've been smacked with guys who wouldn't usually visit Girls Chase – or, if they found us, wouldn't long stay to participate or read. In recent years we've referred to various strains of frustrated men as ‘red pill' (not all red pill men are frustrated, but many are), ‘black pill', ‘incel', ‘looksmaxx'; many different names. Yet there's another name that just as aptly captures all these various average, frustrated men under a single appellation: the Average Frustrated Chump (AFC). Below I'll help you realize if you are one – and if so, what to do! We're Bringing ‘AFC' Back The term Average Frustrated Chump, or AFC, dates to the early days of the seduction community. Title: Getting Tested for STIs: The Active Dater's Guide | Girls Chase
chunks: If you're actively taking on new bedfellows, you should be testing for STIs. How should you test these? Where to do it? When? It's all in this guide. Hey guys. I hope you are doing well. Today, I'll continue my discussion about sexually transmitted infections (STIs). In this article, I will cover STI testing and share the information I have gathered over the years through clinic visits, conversations with specialists, and readings from scientific papers. I encourage you to visit a clinic to learn more from healthcare professionals, and while you're there, consider getting tested. Please remember that this post is not a substitute for professional advice from certified healthcare providers. Testing 101 Testing is important. Don't skip it. For me, testing is the holy grail when it comes to STIs. Whenever you have unprotected sex, you should get tested. The cure to STI worries is through testing. Testing is the best way to ensure good sexual health. You can eliminate the curable infections and drastically reduce the chance of getting the non-curable ones. Note that getting rid of the curable infections decreases contracting the non-curable ones. For more, see part one of this series. It helps ensure your good sexual health and protects others. Testing is THE magic word. It can be scary, but honestly, it is less frightening than you think: You may not have anything (likely), and your mind will be at ease. If you have something, it is usually curable (like gonorrhea or chlamydia). It is less likely that you have syphilis. If you do, you want to eradicate it as quickly as possible. The treatment is typically three injections in your backside over one month.

It is more unlikely that you could have hepatitis C. If you do, you want to eliminate it because serious complications can develop. This involves one to two months of well-tolerated anti-virals. It's very unlikely, but you may contract HIV. This is the scary one that I will devote a section to below. HIV is a severe disease that, if left untreated, leads to AIDS and early death. However, if you have access to treatments, you will not get AIDS, you will not die earlier, and it will not affect your life expectancy. You will also not be contagious after taking the usual treatment for a certain amount of time (usually two to three months). A doctor will sample your blood regularly, and you are not contagious if your doctor cannot detect any virus. You can resume your sex life and not put others at risk. If you are unsure about these details, I encourage you to talk to a healthcare professional. However, the price for having a normal sex life with HIV is that you must take pills daily and get your blood tested often to ensure treatment works and to know whether you are contagious or not. I do not want to trivialize HIV. Do your best to protect yourself. However, one also must be informed and look at it with some nuance: it is not the end of the world. Untreated HIV is not only very contagious, as you put others at serious risk, but extremely dangerous for you. The more you wait, the worse your prognosis is. HIV will not damage your system immediately, but if you wait too long, it may cause irreversible damage. If you take the correct treatment before it causes damage, you can mitigate this.

The bottom line is that you are better off by getting tested. Here is why: If you get tested for HIV, you will clear your mind and know that you don't have it, or find out you have it, and significantly reduce its effects by getting treatment. If you do not get tested, you will keep wondering and worrying, and if you are positive, you contaminate others and eventually destroy your immune system. So, get tested. Where to Test? Specialized STI clinics are an excellent choice. Visit your general practitioner. If a doctor is judgmental, change doctors. If your doctor is not judgmental and you are comfortable with them, they can do the testing or prescribe a battery of tests for you. This is totally fine. I can understand that this can be uncomfortable for some. If so, head to a specialty clinic. They are usually anonymous and free. Most importantly, they are highly specialized. The latter is the reason why I prefer them to my doctor. Specialty clinic professionals have cutting-edge knowledge, and aside from testing and treating, their role is to educate others. It's how I acquired much of my STI knowledge. Ask them in-depth questions. They usually know the answers; if they don't, they know someone who does. They can give you the latest facts, which can really help if you are worried. Be open and talk with them. The vibe there can sometimes be shady, and the clientele can be questionable. But this is good because you will feel more comfortable opening up knowing you have many people in that waiting room who are likely much more hardcore than you are. You are likely not like them and trust me, I know. I had a friend who was an HIV specialist at a clinic.

The stories he relayed were at the next level (note that he never shared patient details or anything that could out them). So, you can feel comfortable with these healthcare providers. Some general practitioners are not up-to-date on infectious diseases like the specialty clinics are. This is because they are not specialists. You cannot blame them. The issue is that they can give you outdated details. One doctor told me I had to wait two to three months before testing for HIV, and that's not correct today. It may have been valid years ago. So, I recommend going to a specialty clinic. The benefit of going to a general practitioner is the shorter waiting time. The waiting time in free public clinics is quite long. If you have limited time, go to your GP. Unless you already have a good foundation about STI facts, I recommend heading to the clinics and using the visit to educate yourself thoroughly. Once you know the drill, you can take shortcuts through your GP (you will likely have to pay). What to Test For? All the good ones. What should you ask the specialist to test you for? Here are the MUSTS. Chlamydia Gonorrhea Syphilis Ask for a hepatitis B test if you are not vaccinated. They can test to see if you have been vaccinated, so healthcare professionals can discard a positive test if vaccinated. You can ask for a test for HIV-1 and HIV-2. (Most tests today test for both. I have not encountered a test for only one.) If you can, test for hepatitis C and mycoplasma. If they offer it, say yes; if they don't, request it. Typically, clinics only test for hepatitis C once yearly, but sometimes, asking will suffice for testing regularly.

You may omit mycoplasma if you are asymptomatic, but if they offer it, get the test. Note that specialty clinics will likely not test for herpes (HSV) and warts (HPV) unless you have an outbreak. If you do, they might diagnose you from visual inspection and take a sample (scrubbing) for testing. However, they may not test unless you have symptoms. You can test for herpes through a blood test to see if you have the virus. However, your GP will do this and not the specialty clinic. I do not recommend this as a routine test unless a professional requests it. The test results may be insignificant. You are likely positive (most people have herpes), and if you are, there is not much you can do, and there's no guarantee that you will experience outbreaks. This may be a pointless test. The mononucleosis test, which one can catch from sleeping around (but even from drinking from other people's cups), is unlikely to be offered by an STI clinic. You will have to go to your general practitioner. There is no need to test for it unless you are symptomatic. When to Test? Checking at the right time interval is crucial. Here are the incubation periods for each STI: Chlamydia: 7–21 days (Most clinics suggest testing after around 7-10 days) Gonorrhea: 1–14 days (most clinics suggest a testing after around 7 days) Syphilis: 10–90 days (most clinics suggest testing after one month, and again after three months if symptomatic, and regularly test if sexually active) Hepatitis B: 21–150 days (most clinics will suggest testing after four weeks of exposure and frequent testing if sexually active and unvaccinated) Hepatitis C: 10 to 90 days (most clinics suggest testing after one month and suggest retesting if sexually active or at risk)

HIV: 14 to 90 days (most clinics suggest testing after six weeks; this is the recommendation in Europe) There are debates about these time windows; variations between countries and clinics will occur. Here are the guidelines from the CDC: https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/yellowbook/2024/posttravel-evaluation/sexually-transmitted-infections If you test before the incubation window, chances are that your test will be a false negative. It may indicate negative, but you are infected, giving you a false sense of security. Here are a few good rules of thumb: If you have had unprotected sex and want to get tested, do it after six weeks. Most tests are reliable after six weeks. If, after intercourse, you test yourself after six weeks, you can be rest assured that you are okay. If you have symptoms like pain in your testicles, pain while urinating, or discharge from your penis, see your doctor and get examined and tested, even before six weeks. You likely have gonorrhea or chlamydia. And if you don't, you may still have a non-sexually transmitted urinary tract infection, which still needs treatment. If you get a rash or round, open sores in your pubic area, get looked at and tested. It may be syphilis. Cold-like symptoms may be symptoms of HIV and do not warrant special attention. Just get tested after six weeks unless the symptoms are unbearable, like a high fever. No Shortcuts There are no home kits for HIV testing and no home test for chlamydia. Some that you buy online are questionable. Even those you see in pharmacies are less precise than lab tests. So, forget about other options as they are unreliable. Do you want to get a false negative, or worse, a false positive HIV result from a home kit? It's not worth it. Do lab tests through a healthcare provider. No shortcuts.

When getting a clinic HIV test, request the fourth-generation AB/AG test that tests for antibodies and antigens. This test is more reliable with fewer false negatives, and you can test earlier. The “wait two months before testing” for HIV is for older test generations. Most clinics offer the newer, fourth-generation test. Beware of “rapid tests,” like saliva or quick tests from drawing blood from a finger. Only get the needle-in-the-arm tests performed in a clinic or laboratory. What About HIV Testing? If you have a serious HIV scare, it can be difficult to wait six weeks. The worries may be unbearable. I have good news, however. Waiting six weeks is ideal for HIV testing, and the reliability is close to 100% (Remember that 0% and 100% do not exist in medicine). But, I can live with 99% after 44 days, and most medical professionals will conclude that you do not have HIV and will not need retesting. Testing again is warranted if doctors consider you at high risk for exposure, like if you had sex with someone who just got diagnosed positively. Remember, the six-week window applies only to fourth-generation AB/AG needle-in-the-arm tests. If you cannot wait six weeks, you can get tested after two weeks. You may do this if you think you are infected, as the antigen (p24) shows up on blood tests after approximately two to three weeks. They may decrease after four to eight weeks, and it's why the fourth generation also tests for antibodies. If infected, positive results appear after three to four weeks and stay detectable for the rest of your life. This means you could detect HIV after two weeks with a reasonable success rate and almost perfectly detect HIV after six weeks.

Testing after two to three weeks is okay if you want to calm your nerves and get an idea of where you are. If you are negative after two to three weeks, you likely do not have HIV. However, this will not clear you. A test after two to three weeks is not enough. It can give you a good indicator. If you are negative, you likely do not have HIV, but you cannot tell for sure. Retest after four weeks to be certain. At this point, you can move on. Note: You can technically test for HIV after seven to ten days with an RNA Quantitative (viral load) test. These tests are expensive and not reliable for diagnosis. Doctors typically administer these to monitor HIV patients already diagnosed. However, if your paranoia is at the next level, you can do an antigenic test and an RNA test after two weeks. If both are negative, you can be reasonably sure you do not have HIV. However, you should still get retested after four weeks. For more details, see https://i-base.info/guides/testing/what-is-the-window-period and https://www.aidsmap.com/about-hiv/what-window-period-hiv-testing Parting Words You'll feel a lot more confident when you know you're in the clear. Whenever you have unprotected sex, you should test yourself after six weeks (and earlier if you experience symptoms). I usually advise anyone to test themselves at least once a year. For sexually active men, I advise testing three to four times a year, usually three to four months apart, but test right away whenever you have symptoms and then test more often. I have a routine test every three to four months. Most health authorities recommend this time frame for at-risk groups. These groups include men who have sex with men, prostitutes, drug users, and transgender people.

However, although less discussed, sexually active heterosexuals also fall within this category. So, it is better to get tested four times a year. My recommendation to you is to get tested at a clinic soon if you haven't been tested in a while, using the occasion to discuss your sexual history with an expert and create a plan for how often you should get tested (they will likely suggest a less stringent protocol than mine). Utilize those health professionals to develop the best plan for your sexual health. This is the way to go about it. It is better to test too much than too little. If you are unsure whether you should get tested, do it. It's that simple. Stay safe, Alek
